messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
Bram listens to the whole of it with the sword point in the dirt, and when Vosk is done he's quiet for the length of a breath.

"It's enough." He slides the longsword home. "Not because I like the answer. Because you gave it without me having to dig, and because the mule's looking at the firewood and not the wagon. That's the test I set, and it's passed, tonight. We'll set it again every night from here to the Gate, and I'll be awake for the next one." A short nod toward the stalls. "But hear this, Master Vosk, and take it for the last time I say it kindly: on the road, you don't wait to be asked. Mules pull a picket, frost on a lid, a clerk in grey — you tell me when it happens, not when I catch you at it. I can't stand in the right place for a thing I've not been told about. You held back once to keep me. Hold back twice and you'll lose me, and you'll lose me at the worst mile on the Way."

Then he turns to Pim on the threshold.

"Lift the bar, lad. One leaf, wide enough for a man." He looks at Harn. "Up. Slow. Knife when you're through, not before — I'll kick it out after you." He waits until Harn's moved off the tailboard before he adds, "And Harn. The Amnian said it better than I did. What you knew was never worth anything to a sergeant. It was worth something to the kind of man who doesn't wear a badge, and you'd have gone looking for him sober. Be glad you were drunk." He watches the man through the gap, kicks the sheathed knife after him into the lane, and tells Pim: "Bar it. Then bed."

To Pell, once the bar's down: "You did well. Knee was a hair high, but the logs did the rest, and nobody bled." He picks the scattered split oak up two at a time and leans it back under the low board, the same careless balance as before. "Your watch still. Wake me at grey."

And to Vosk, as the factor turns for the door, quieter: "Go back to bed. Whatever's in that box didn't stir for any of this. I'm starting to think it's not the box we need to watch on this road. It's who's heard of it."

He settles back against the wheel, shield across his lap, and closes his eyes.

 — to first light, unless the yard objects.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell keeps his place between Harn and the fence, letting Bram and Vosk talk it out. He listens with the same close quiet he's held all night, turning Vosk's words over for the seams.

When Vosk finishes, Pell glances toward the stable, where the mule's ears are up and its eyes are on the logs, not the wagon. Then he looks back at Bram. "I've got this side," he says, low. "Say the word and the gate opens." He doesn't move for the bar, and he doesn't take his eyes off Harn, but the offer's plain. His own back is to the dark lane, the woodpile's spilled logs at his heels, and he seems in no hurry to leave the yard.

scenes.narration:
"It's enough."

Bram slides the longsword home. Vosk watches the blade go into the scabbard and lets out a breath he has plainly been holding since the stairs. He hears the rest out with the candle-lamp steady: the test set again every night from here to the Gate, and the warning that on the road nobody waits to be asked. Pulled pickets, frost on the lid, a clerk in grey: Bram is to be told when it happens, not when he catches it. He held back once to keep Bram on. Do it twice, and he loses Bram at the worst mile on the Way.

Vosk doesn't argue this time.

"Understood, Master Halloway. When it happens, then. Not when you ask." He says it slowly, like a man writing a clause into a contract he means to keep. "You'll have it at the hour it happens, whatever the hour is."

Bram turns toward the threshold. Before he gets the words out, Pell speaks up from the fence side, low, his eyes still on Harn. "I've got this side. Say the word and the gate opens." He doesn't move toward the bar.

Bram gives the word to Pim. *Lift the bar, lad. One leaf, wide enough for a man.*

"One leaf, wide enough for a man." Pim is across the yard before he finishes repeating it. He has to get his shoulder under the bar to shift it out of the brackets, and he lays it carefully on the ground so it won't bang. Then he drags one leaf of the gate inward, and its bottom edge scrapes across the packed earth. Past the gap the Coast Way is grey and empty, and every door along it is dark.

*Up. Slow.*

Harn pushes himself off the tailboard. The bad hip catches him on the first step, and he walks the rest of the way to the gate stiffly, giving Bram a wide berth. He doesn't look at the middle wagon. Pell turns where he stands to keep him in view and lets him pass.

At the gap Bram tells him the rest: what he knew was never worth anything to a sergeant. It was worth something to the kind of man who doesn't wear a badge, and he'd have gone looking for that man sober.

scenes.input:
(Round 18 — one paragraph per character in this scene. Bram Halloway and Pell Dunmore are elsewhere this round, in a scene of their own that comes to you as its own message: do not narrate them here.)

Sefa Marrin: I continue sleeping until dawn or until something wakes me.
scenes.narration:
Sefa sleeps through the last of the night without waking.

Nothing comes up the stairs. The murmur from the yard on the far side of the house dies away, and after it there's only the cold. Some time before grey a door at the end of the passage opens, and slow, heavy steps come past her room. This time no lamp crosses the crack under her door. The steps go down the stairs, the third tread creaks, then the seventh, and they're gone. She doesn't stir.

What wakes her is the street. Up the Coast Way a cock crows too early and gives up halfway through. Farther off, iron rings twice as someone knocks the night's ash out of a forge. When she opens her eyes, the cracks around the shutter have gone from black to the colour of slate.

The room is very cold. The jug on the washstand has a skin of chill on it, and her breath shows faintly above the blanket. The beads have slid down onto the tick beside her pillow, and the cracked one is as cool as the rest. The book is where she left it, and so are her clothes. The bolt is still shot.

The house is waking around her. In the loft a carter coughs, swears, and somebody's boots hit the floor. Below, a bar scrapes out of its brackets, and Orla's voice says something short to nobody in particular. Pots knock together in the kitchen. Faintly, from the yard side, comes the creak and splash of a bucket at the trough and a mule blowing at the smell of water.

She got a full night's sleep, the whole stretch from the lamps to grey, and she's rested for it.

It isn't full light yet. Vosk said he'd leave at first light, and that's close now. Nothing else happens in Sefa's room unless she makes it happen.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
Bram gets up off the wheel the way he got up off a hundred: slow, knees first, one hand on the spoke. He rolls his shoulders until the mail sits right, then before he says a word to anyone he climbs onto the middle wagon's bench, unties the two front lashings and folds the canvas back a hand's width.

He looks at the lid. He puts his palm flat on it, then on the linen bolt beside it. Whatever he finds, he says it aloud, plain, to Vosk in the doorway: dry or wet, cold or not, frost or none. Then he ties the lashings again and climbs down.

"Night's report," he says. "One man over the fence, sent off up the street. The box did nothing a box shouldn't. Mules slept." He nods at the end stall. "That's the first of four. Three more to go."

He turns to Pell, and doesn't speak for him.

"He's waiting on you, Dunmore. Not me. Say it or don't, but say it before the mules are in the shafts, because once they are I stop counting heads." Then, to Vosk: "Half when we start, you said. I'll take mine before the first wheel turns, and I'll want bread with it — Orla's, not hardtack. And the healer upstairs doesn't know we're leaving unless someone's told her. I'll knock on my way to the privy. She turned your coin down, that's her right, but I'd not walk north without saying so to her face. Ten minutes, and I'll be at the lead team's head."

He slings the shield onto his back for the moment, picks up the guttered candle-lamp from the dirt and hands it to Vosk in passing.

"Yours. It did its job."

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell stays where he has been, back against the cold stable wall, the night's work settled into his shoulders but his eyes still clear. He watches Vosk stand in the doorway and lets the quiet run a moment longer before he speaks.

"Quiet since the gate was barred." He nods once toward the fence, where the logs lean untouched. "Nobody came back for a second try."

He shifts off the wall and stands at his ease, wincing only slightly as he rolls one shoulder where Harn elbowed him. "You're abroad before the crowing," he says to Vosk. "First light's not far. I'll wash the yard off my hands and be down to give you my word."

scenes.narration:
Bram gets up off the wheel slowly, knees first, one hand on a spoke. The cold has settled into the mail overnight, and he rolls his shoulders until it hangs right. Then he climbs onto the middle wagon's bench, where Vosk sat yesterday, works the two front lashings loose and folds the canvas back a hand's width.

The grey light reaches the crate. There is no frost on it. He lays his palm flat on the lid, and the oak is cold. It is colder than the bench under his knee and colder than the iron band an inch from his fingers, as if the wood had spent the night somewhere else. The hum comes up into his hand the same as it did last night, no stronger and no weaker. He moves his hand to the bolt of linen pressed against the crate's far side. It is wet now, not just damp, and the wet has spread a finger's width further into the cloth than it was by lamplight.

He tells Vosk exactly that across the yard: no frost, the lid cold, the linen wetter than last night, and the hum unchanged. Then he ties the lashings off again and climbs down.

Vosk hears it from the doorway, and his mouth goes tight. "Wetter," he says, as if he were writing it in a margin. "I'll have that bolt moved to the tail of the first wagon before we yoke. It is spoiled for selling as it is." He doesn't argue the rest.

*Night's report.* Bram gives it in four short pieces: one man over the fence and sent off up the street, the box doing nothing a box shouldn't, the mules asleep, and one night down with three to go.

Pell comes off the stable wall as Bram finishes. He rolls the shoulder Harn's elbow found and winces a little.

"Quiet since the gate was barred." He nods toward the fence, where the six logs still lean against each other. "Nobody came back for a second try." Then, to Vosk: "You're abroad before the crowing. First light's not far. I'll wash the yard off my hands and be down to give you my word."

Vosk looks at him for a moment, then at the sky over the stable roof. It is slate, going pale at the eastern edge.

"Wash, then, Master Dunmore. The mules go into the shafts when I can read the ledger without a lamp." He doesn't say *and not after*, but it is plain in how he says it.

Bram turns to Pell and leaves the choice with him. He's waiting on you, not me. Say it before the mules are in the shafts, because after that Bram stops counting heads. Then he turns to Vosk: half when we start, his before the first wheel turns, and bread from Orla's kitchen, not hardtack.

Vosk opens the ledger against his forearm, takes a small purse from inside his coat and counts four gold pieces into Bram's hand without hurrying.

"Four days at two, the half of it is four. Paid." He marks the page with his pen, and this time the nib is wet. "The bread is part of your food, Master Halloway. That is mine to buy, not yours. I'll have Mistress Tarnwick put up a loaf for each man and a round of cheese. She'll be glad of the custom before breakfast."

Bram also tells him that the healer upstairs doesn't know they're leaving unless somebody tells her, and that he'll knock on her door himself. She turned the coin down, which is her right, but he won't walk north without saying it to her face. Vosk nods slowly.

"That is decent of you. She was decent to me." He closes the ledger. "Second door on the left. You know it."

Bram slings the shield onto his back, picks Vosk's candle-lamp up out of the straw and puts it in the factor's hand as he goes past. *Yours. It did its job.*

Vosk looks down at the cold glass with its burnt-out thread of tallow, and for a moment something close to a smile shows under the grey beard. "So it did."

At the trough Pim has stopped pouring and is listening with his mouth half open. Vosk raises his voice to him. "Pim. The middle team first, then the lead. Harness, not yoke. Not until I say."

"Middle team first, then the lead. Harness, not yoke." The boy says it into the bucket and goes into the stable at a trot.

Bram goes in through the yard door. The common room smells of new smoke and bread. Orla is at the hearth with a poker and doesn't look round, and the stairs are ahead of him.

*(Out of game: Bram's knock on Sefa's door happens in Sefa's scene, so her answer comes from her player there.)*

1) I didn't roll for the crate: putting a hand on a lid and a bolt of cloth and saying what you feel can't go wrong, so the story gave the result straight: no frost, the lid cold, the linen wetter, the hum the same.

2) I didn't roll for the knock either. Bram is on his way to Sefa's door now, and since she's in her own scene, the knock and whatever she says back belong to her scene.

messages.text:
I wash quickly in the cold water, dress, and buckle on my armour. I tuck the prayer beads into place, secure the Book of Shadows at my belt, and gather my pack before unbolting the door.

Downstairs, I give Orla a quiet good morning, then head into the yard to see whether Bram and Pell are still there.

scenes.narration:
The water in the chipped jug is cold enough to sting. Sefa splashes her face and the back of her neck, and her breath clouds over the basin. She dresses fast, the way people do in a room where the shutter's cracks have only just gone grey, and buckles on the studded leather, which is stiff from the night. The beads go round her neck with the cracked one sitting where it always sits. It is cool against her collarbone. The pale-bound book goes onto her belt, warm the way its pages always are. She shoulders the pack and draws the bolt, and it slides back with the same solid knock it made going home.

The passage is grey and smells of tallow. The door across the hall stands open a crack on an empty, unmade bed. From the loft come coughing, a boot hunting for its pair and somebody swearing. Down below, pots knock together in the kitchen, and the smell of new bread is coming up the stairwell.

She's three steps from the stairhead when the third step creaks under someone coming up.

It's a heavy tread, slow, and mail chinks with it. A shape climbs out of the stairwell's dark toward the grey light at the top: a broad-shouldered man with a round shield slung on his back, coming up to her floor. He's between her and the common room, a few steps below the seventh tread.

*(Out of game: Bram was coming up the stairs to knock on her door, so the two scenes meet here on the stairs. I've stopped at that moment so Bram's player can say what he does, and the round can go on from there with both of them.)*

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
Bram takes the stairs, lets the third and seventh steps creak because there's no helping it, and stops at the second door on the left. He knocks twice with a knuckle, not loud — the kind of knock that says *it's not trouble, but it's not nothing either*.

"Mistress Marrin. Halloway. Vosk's yoking in a quarter hour and I said I'd not go north without telling you to your face."

If she opens, he stands back from the door and keeps it short.

"Night's news, since some of it's yours. Harn came over the fence past midnight. Drunk, bad hip, hand on a knife he never drew. Dunmore and I had him on his knees before he'd got a boot down, and he talked. He loaded that crate himself at the Nashkel forfeit house, back door before sunup, clerk in grey. He couldn't read the seal — thought it was excise. He meant to look, then squeeze Vosk for silence money. I sent him up the street with his knife and a warning. Nobody bled."

"And the box. No frost this morning. But the lid's colder than the iron bands on it, and the linen beside it's wetter than it was by lamplight — spread a finger's width. The hum's the same. The mules slept through all of it, bar the logs falling." He shifts the shield on his back. "You said it's the cold that wants explaining, not the water. It's getting colder, and it's doing it in a stable with no wind. I thought you'd want that for whatever you make of it."

Then, plainly: "You turned the coin down and I'll not argue it. But you came down that road and you've nowhere to be, as far as I heard. If you're walking north anyway, paid or not, there's bread and cheese going into the first wagon and you'd be welcome to walk beside it. If you're staying, then good luck in Beregost and thank you for reading the wax. That's all. I'll be at the lead team's head."

He waits for whatever she says, then goes down: the privy, a splash from the trough, Orla's bread, and his place at the lead mule's head with the shield on his arm.

The man on the stairs comes up into the grey light from the stairhead's one small window, and Sefa can see his face: Bram, with the shield slung on his back and straw on the shoulders of his mail. He has a night's stubble and looks like he slept on the ground.

"Good morning. Bram?"

He stops two treads short of the top so he isn't crowding her on the landing. Below him a carter comes out of the loft passage with his boots in his hand, squeezes past with a grunt and goes on down. The seventh step creaks under him.

"Mistress Marrin. Halloway." He nods at the door behind her, the one he'd been going to knock on. "Saves me a knock. Vosk's yoking in a quarter hour, and I said I'd not go north without telling you to your face."

He keeps it short and level, the way he gave the factor his report in the yard.

"Night's news, since some of it's yours. Harn came over the fence past midnight. Drunk, bad hip, hand on a knife he never drew. From below comes the smell of new bread and the clatter of the kitchen. He shifts the shield's strap on his shoulder.

"And the box. No frost this morning. But the lid's colder than the iron bands on it, and the linen beside it's wetter than it was by lamplight, spread a finger's width. The hum's the same. messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell walks to the trough, rolls up his sleeves, and washes the yard off his hands and face with a few quick splashes of icy water. He dries them on the hem of his shirt and shakes the stiffness out of his wrists.

Then he crosses to where Vosk stands with the ledger, and says it plainly: "I'm in. Two gold a day, food, half now and half at the Basilisk Gate." A short nod toward the yard and the gate. "I'll take my place where Bram can see me, and I'll keep my hands on the outside of the wagons."

He holds his palm out without any flourish. "I'll take my four now, same as him."

scenes.narration:
Pell rolls his sleeves back and plunges his hands into the trough. The water is cold enough to make his wrists ache, and the night's grit and old straw lift off his skin. Two quick splashes to his face clear the last of the watch out of his eyes. He wipes himself on the hem of his shirt and shakes his hands out. From inside the stable comes the clink of buckles as Pim works, and the middle team blows and shifts under the harness.

Vosk is still standing in the yard door with the ledger under his arm. The grey over the stable roof is turning pale at its eastern edge, and he watches Pell walk the whole way across the yard to him.

"I'm in. Two gold a day, food, half now and half at the Basilisk Gate." Pell tips his head toward the gate and the wagons. "I'll take my place where Bram can see me, and I'll keep my hands on the outside of the wagons." He holds out his open palm. "I'll take my four now, same as him."

For a moment Vosk only looks at the hand. Then he opens the ledger against his forearm and takes the small purse out of his coat again. He counts four gold pieces into Pell's palm one at a time, and his eyes stay on Pell's face until the last coin is down.

"Four. Paid." He turns to the page, writes a short line under Bram's and blots it with his thumb. "You are counted, Master Dunmore. Where you walk on the road, Master Halloway will say. That is his trade, and I will not set his line for him." He closes the ledger. "You stood the watch alone after he slept. Pim tells me nobody came back down the lane." It isn't thanks, quite. It's a figure he has noted and means to keep.

His glance drops to the earthenware bowl on the straw by the stable wall, scraped clean.

"And Mistress Tarnwick's bowl goes back to her kitchen before we roll. I will not leave this town owing her crockery."

He steps back over the threshold toward the smell of bread and Orla's voice. Behind Pell the stable door bangs open. Pim backs out leading the first of the middle team, harnessed but not yet in the shafts. The mule plants its feet on the packed earth and blows at the cold. It doesn't so much as look at the middle wagon.

It's still a little short of full light. Nothing else is asked of Pell before the yoking unless he wants something.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
Bram stays on his tread with his hand on the rail and doesn't add to it. He's said his piece; a man who keeps talking after that is trying to sell something, and he isn't.

He only says, after a moment, quieter: "Take your time deciding, but not much of it. Vosk reads his ledger without a lamp, the mules go in. I've seen the sky — that's a quarter hour, no more."

Then he waits for her answer, and whatever it is, he nods to it, goes back down past the creaking steps, and gets on with the morning: privy, cold water from the trough on his face and neck, Orla's loaf and cheese for the first wagon, and his place at the lead mule's head with the shield on his arm and his eyes on the gate.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
“Thank you for coming up. And I’m glad nobody bled.”

I shift my pack on my shoulder.

“I’m staying. Walking beside the wagon without taking pay wouldn’t make my doubts about it any smaller.”

My eyes drop briefly to the straw caught in his mail. “You kept your word last night. Keep the condition you gave him, too. If someone wakes cold, stop. Don’t let him bargain you another mile before you do.”

I move aside to clear the landing. “I may try High Hedge by daylight. There’s something worth learning here, even if I never see that crate again.”

Then I offer him my hand. “Safe road, Bram. If we meet in the Gate, I’d be glad to share a table again.”

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell closes his hand over the four gold, drops them into his purse without counting, and gives Vosk a small nod. "Counted, then."

He stoops for the bowl by the stable wall, knocks the straw dust from it, and follows a few steps behind the factor toward the door. "I'll put this back in the kitchen before we roll," he says, half to Vosk, half to the morning.

Before he goes in, he pauses in the doorway and takes one last look across the yard: the middle wagon, the mule already out and not even glancing at it, the logs still leaning under the fence. Then he slips inside, moving through the warm, bread-smelling dimness toward the kitchen to hand over Orla's bowl and see if there's hot bread, weak ale, and any word of Sefa coming down.

scenes.narration:
The four gold go into Pell's purse without a sound. "Counted, then." Vosk nods once and is already turning toward the smell of bread.

Pell picks the bowl up off the straw and knocks it against his palm to shake the dust out. "I'll put this back in the kitchen before we roll."

He stops on the threshold and looks back at the yard. The first mule of the middle team stands harnessed by the trough. It blows at the cold and keeps its head turned toward Pim and the stable, nowhere near the middle wagon. The canvas on that wagon is lashed tight again. Past the third wagon the six logs still lean against each other under the low board. Over the stable roof the slate has a pale edge to it now.

Inside, the common room is dim and warm. Someone has raked the hearth up, and the first flames are licking at new wood. The benches are empty except for a carter asleep sitting up with his cheek on his folded arms. The kitchen passage smells of yeast and smoke. Vosk is halfway down it, telling someone through the doorway what he wants in exact figures: "A loaf for each man, a round of cheese. Wrapped, if you would."

Orla is at the long board in the kitchen with her sleeves pushed up, pulling loaves out of the oven mouth on a peel. She doesn't stop for Vosk. "A loaf a man and a round of cheese. You'll have them by the time your mules are in." Then she sees Pell behind him with the bowl.

She takes it out of his hands, turns it over once and looks at the inside, which is scraped clean. "Well. You ate it cold." It doesn't sound like a complaint. The bowl goes onto a stack of others by the wash-tub. "That's your tab square, Master Dunmore. Pim gave me your silver last night, and the copper he kept, I'd guess." Her eyes go briefly to the common room. "Your mug's still on my mantel. Bring it on your way out and we're quits."

She sets the peel against the oven wall and wipes her hands down her apron. "Hot bread's a copper a heel if you want it now and not on the road. Small beer's two coppers the cup, and it's weak, before you ask." She jerks her chin at the ceiling. "Nobody's come down from upstairs but carters. Your shield man went up a few minutes back, and not toward the loft."

Behind her the loaves sit steaming on the board. Vosk waits in the passage with his ledger under his arm, watching the window over the wash-tub. It's getting lighter.

Nobody needs anything more from Pell before the mules go in, unless he wants something.

 *(Out of game, one line each:)*

1) Vosk paid Pell, not the other way round: he counted four gold into Pell's hand last round, and Pell put it in his purse this turn. Handing the bowl back to Orla couldn't go wrong, so it needed no roll, and the story shows it done.

2) Pell went in to *see* whether there was hot bread and weak ale. He didn't say he was buying any, so Orla gave him the prices (a copper a heel, two coppers a cup) and his player decides whether he buys. She did answer the question about Sefa: nobody has come down but carters, and Bram went up a few minutes ago.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
Bram takes the hand. His is big and rough and cold from the yard, and he doesn't crush hers; he shakes it once, the way he'd shake a hand over a finished deal.

"Staying's a fair answer. Better than walking a road you don't believe in." He lets go. "And I'll keep the condition. Someone wakes cold, we stop. He'll argue — he's told me so twice — and I'll let him, and then we'll stop anyway. I've been bargained an extra mile before. It's a mile too far every time."

He glances once at the straw on his own mail, as she did, and brushes at it without much effect.

"High Hedge. If the old man opens his gate to you, ask him about the circle with three strokes. The one someone scraped off before Nashkel. Vosk doesn't know it, Harn couldn't read it, and you didn't know it either, which makes it the only thing on that box nobody's got a story for." A short pause. "I'm the last man to tell a healer her business. But if it was mine I'd want that answered before the wax."

He steps down a tread to give her the landing.

"Safe road to you too, Mistress Marrin. The Elfsong, if I'm in the Gate and standing — I'll be the one with his back to the wall." Then he goes down, the third and seventh steps creaking under him, and out through the yard door into the grey, to the privy, the trough, the loaf and cheese, and the lead mule's head, shield on his arm and eyes on the gate.

messages.text:
“My mind’s made up, Bram. I’m staying in Beregost today.”

I leave my hand offered for the farewell. “Good luck to you.”

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell pulls three coppers from his purse and sets them on the board's edge. "Hot bread and a cup. Weak's fine." He takes the heel Orla passes him, wraps it mostly in his fingers rather than his palm, and stands just clear of the kitchen doorway where the heat pours past him and he isn't in anyone's road.

He eats the bread slowly, blowing over each bite more from habit than need. Between mouthfuls he tracks the sounds of the house: the clink behind him in the kitchen, the scrape and thump of men dressing and coming down the stairs, any sign of Sefa's voice. In the yard, Pim's low steady cursing at a harness strap carries through with the first scrape of the yoking.

He finishes the bread, knuckles the crumbs off his hands, and takes his weak ale by the cup. Then he moves back toward the low end of the common room, where the carter still sleeps, and stands where he can watch both the stair and the front door.

scenes.narration:
Orla scoops the three coppers off the edge of the board without counting them. She breaks a heel off the end of the nearest loaf, steam and all, and holds it out on her flat palm. Then she draws a cup of small beer from the cask under the window and sets it beside his hand. "One and two. Square." She has already turned back to the oven.

The heel is too hot to hold properly, so Pell holds it in his fingertips. He stands just clear of the doorway, where the oven's heat rolls out past him into the cold passage and he isn't in anyone's way. The crust cracks when he bites it. The inside is soft and grey-white, and it tastes of the oven more than of salt. The beer is weak, as she said, thin and a little sour, and cold from the cask.

The house goes on around him. Behind him a pot lid rings on the board and Orla tells the fire something short. Upstairs, boots go across the loft, a door bangs and a carter laughs at somebody. Out in the yard, through two doors and a passage, Pim is talking to a harness strap in a low, steady mutter that never quite becomes words. There's the knock of a tongue being lifted, and a mule blows.

Halfway through the heel, the stairs speak. It's a heavy tread. The seventh step creaks, then the third, and mail chinks with each step. Bram comes off the bottom stair with straw still on his shoulders and the shield slung on his back. He doesn't look round the common room. He turns at the foot of the stairs toward the yard door and goes out through it, and the cold comes in around the door for a moment before it shuts.

Nobody comes down after him. Up at the top of the stairs it's quiet. It isn't a sleeping quiet. Someone is standing up there, but they say nothing Pell can hear.

He finishes the bread and knocks the crumbs off his knuckles. He carries the cup down to the low end of the common room, past the hearth. The new flames are taking the wood properly now. On the mantel above it, his empty cider mug from last night is still standing where he left it. The carter is still asleep sitting up at the end bench, his cheek on his folded arms and his breath whistling. From where Pell stands now, he can see the foot of the stairs and the front door onto the Coast Way. The door is still barred. The grey through its cracks has turned the colour of milk.

Out in the yard Vosk is waiting for him. Nothing else calls Pell before then unless he wants it to.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
Bram runs a hand down the lead mule's neck, finds the harness buckle at the collar and gives it a tug to be sure Pim's drawn it tight, then checks the trace on the near side. Old habit. He'd do it on a run he trusted and he'll do it twice on this one.

"The fourth read your wax for you and asked nothing for it," he says to Vosk, not looking up from the buckle. "That's more than Harn did for his two days. Don't count her against you." He straightens. "And when Dunmore comes out, he walks the middle wagon's off side where I can see him from the lead, and you sit the middle bench where you always do. scenes.narration:
The buckle at the lead mule's collar holds when Bram tugs it, and so does the near-side trace. Pim drew both tight, and he did it right, with the tongue of the strap tucked back under its keeper. The mule turns its head round at Bram's hand and blows warm breath against his mail, then loses interest.

Vosk stands by the first wagon's tail with the ledger under his arm and hears Bram out. At *the fourth* his eyes go up to the window again.

"I don't count her against me, Master Halloway. She looked at the crate when nobody asked her to, and she told me the truth about what she couldn't see. I would rather have that from her than a yes she didn't mean." Then the drill, and he takes it the same way he took the terms last night, point by point. "The middle bench, as always. You call the halt, and the lead stops first. Nobody passes the lead. Agreed."

He shifts the ledger.

"On Master Dunmore, though, you are a quarter hour behind. He gave me his yes in this yard while you were on the stairs. Plain terms, the same as yours, and he took his four." He glances at the yard door. "He went in with Mistress Tarnwick's bowl. When he comes out, we are ready."

At *the sergeant's breakfast* the corner of his mouth tightens. "The north post is a corporal at this hour, and in my experience he is curious about everything until he has seen a stamp and a few silver. I'll do the talking there, if you don't object. It goes quicker when the man asking the questions is the man with the paper."

Behind them Pim comes out of the stable leading the second lead mule. He backs it up beside its partner, talking to the harness under his breath, and starts on the collar buckle without being told. The middle team stands quiet in the shafts. A faint hum comes up through the middle wagon's boards into the tongue and the traces, and neither mule pays it any mind.

The light over the stable roof has gone from pale grey to plain morning. The logs still lean against the fence, and the bar is still down across the gate. All they're waiting on now is the yard door.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
I go downstairs and find Orla.

“Good morning. What do I owe for bread, cheese and something hot? And which turning takes me onto the High Hedge road?”

Over breakfast, I try to fix the scraped sigil in my memory, keeping what I actually saw separate from what the missing strokes might have been. I won’t improve it by guessing.

Once I’ve eaten and paid, I set out west in daylight. I intend to approach High Hedge openly, by the road, and ask whether Thalantyr receives visitors seeking advice on a magical mark—and what he charges for the consultation.

scenes.narration:
Sefa comes down the stairs with her pack on her shoulder. The third step creaks under her, then the seventh. The common room is warmer than the landing. The hearth has caught properly, the benches are mostly empty, and a carter sleeps sitting up at the end bench with his cheek on his arms. At the low end of the room, near the fire, Pell Dunmore stands with a cup in his hand.

Orla is in the kitchen with her sleeves pushed up, knocking loaves out of their tins onto the board. She looks up when Sefa reaches the doorway.

"Good morning. What do I owe for bread, cheese and something hot? And which turning takes me onto the High Hedge road?"

"Hot bread's a copper a heel. Cheese is two the wedge. Hot is cider, five, the same pot as last night, and it's better for sitting." Orla breaks a heel off the end loaf and puts it on a board, cuts a wedge from a round under a cloth and sets it beside the bread. She ladles cider from the pot at the hearth's edge into a clay mug. "Eight coppers. Sit where you like, there's room now."

She wipes her knife on her apron and points it at the front of the house.

"Out the front, turn right, down the Way toward the temple end. Past the last smithy there's a horse trough where the road splits. The left fork goes west. That's your road. Stay on it and you'll see the hedge before you see the house. It's that kind of hedge." She has turned back to her tins already. "An hour, if you don't stop to look at things."

Sefa sits at the near end of the long table. The bread is too hot to tear cleanly. The cheese is hard and sharp, and the cider tastes of clove, warm through the clay. Between mouthfuls she goes over the mark the way she would go over a dressing she had to describe to the sister on the next shift: only what was there. A burned circle on the end board, low down. Three short strokes cutting into it that don't meet in the middle. More than half of it scraped away, the scrape lines grey and old. She doesn't know how many strokes there were before the blade went over them, or where they ran. She leaves that part blank.

She counts eight coppers onto the board by the kitchen door. Orla sweeps them into her apron without turning round. "Square."

---

The front door opens onto the Coast Way in plain morning light. The street smells of fresh coal smoke. Down the road the first forges are opening their shutters, and a smith's boy is throwing ash into the gutter by the bucketful. A cart goes north loaded with barrel staves. Sefa turns right, toward the temple end, as Orla said. She walks past the cooper's shop and four smithies with their doors open and the hammers just starting. At the last one the road widens around a stone horse trough with a skin of cold on the water, and splits.

The left fork runs west out of town between low stone walls, and Beregost falls behind her quickly. The hammering thins until it sounds like a clock in another room, then it's gone. There are fields on both sides, stubble and dark ploughed earth with frost still white in the furrows on the shaded side. A crow walks in one of them and ignores her. Half an hour out, a farmer with a handcart full of turnips comes the other way. He nods to her and says the morning's a cold one, which it is, and goes on toward town. After that she has the road to herself for a long stretch. Her boots are loud on the frozen ruts. The sun comes up behind her and throws her shadow out ahead on the road, long and thin.

Orla was right about the hedge. Sefa sees it a good while before anything else: a dark green wall across the land ahead to the left of the road, too straight and too tall for any farmer's boundary. As she gets closer she can see it's yew, clipped flat on top, easily twice a man's height. It runs a long way in both directions. Over it shows the top of a building, a narrow tower of grey stone with one window facing the road and a thread of smoke going straight up from a chimney in the still air.

A short track leaves the road and runs up to a gap in the yew. In the gap stands a gate of black iron bars, shut. Through the bars she can see a gravel path and more hedge beyond, so she can't see the house from here. Beside the gate an iron bell hangs from a bracket with a pull-chain under it. A small board is nailed to the gatepost, its paint worn but legible:

*CALLERS BY DAYLIGHT. RING ONCE.*

Nobody is at the gate. Somewhere past the hedge a bird calls once and stops. The smoke from the chimney goes on rising. It's a little past a quarter to eight.

*(Out of game: Pell was in the common room when Sefa came down. Anything that passed between them belongs to his player and his scene, so I've only shown where he was standing.)*

 *(Out of game, one line each:)*

1) No roll was needed: buying breakfast at the inn couldn't go wrong. Sefa paid Orla eight coppers and ate.

2) No roll was needed, since she was just asking the way. Orla told her: right down the Way, past the last smithy, then the left fork west at the horse trough.

3) No roll was needed, because Sefa saw the mark herself last night and only remembered what was there. The strokes that were scraped away stay unknown, as she wanted.

4) No roll was needed: walking an hour down an open road in daylight is just travel. She's at High Hedge's gate now, and she hasn't rung the bell yet.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell sets the empty cup on the mantel beside the cider mug from the night before, two clay vessels side by side like bookends to the watch.

Then he glances once toward the top of the stairs. The silence up there is the sort that means someone is listening back. He doesn't call out. He lets his heels fall on the floor as he crosses to the yard door, just enough noise that whoever is standing in the dark upstairs knows he's gone and can make her own choice without an audience.

He eases the door open and steps through. Cold air and the smell of mules and cold iron meet him. He pulls the door to behind him without a bang, then walks toward the middle wagon to see where Bram wants him.

scenes.narration:
Pell sets the empty cup on the mantel beside last night's cider mug. Two clay pots stand side by side above the new fire. The carter at the end bench whistles on in his sleep.

Pell looks once at the top of the stairs. The quiet up there hasn't changed. He doesn't call out. He crosses the floor letting his heels come down, loud enough for anyone on the landing to hear a man leaving, and puts his hand on the latch of the yard door. Behind him the third stair creaks once under a light step. Then he's through the door and pulling it to, and it shuts without a bang.

The yard is cold and smells of mules and wet straw. Above the stable roof it's plain morning now, and the frost has gone grey and soft on the shaded side of the trough. The middle team stands in the shafts. The faint hum comes up through the wagon's tongue and traces, and neither mule pays it any mind. At the far end of the row Pim is on his toes at the second lead mule's collar. He pulls the buckle through, tucks the strap's tongue under its keeper the way Bram checked the first one, and steps back, wiping his hands on his shirt. Bram stands at the lead team's head with the shield on his arm, his eyes on the gate.

Vosk is at the tail of the first wagon with the ledger under his arm. He sees Pell come out and heads him off before he reaches the middle wagon. He keeps his voice low, though there's nobody in the yard who doesn't already know the business.

"Master Dunmore. Master Halloway has set your place while you were inside. The middle wagon's off side, the far side from the stable, where he can see you from the lead. If he calls a halt, the lead stops first and the others close up. Nobody passes the lead." He goes through it the way he'd read a clause back to a buyer. "That is the drill. It's his, not mine."

He looks along the row. The lead team is harnessed, the middle team is in the shafts, and Orla's wrapped bread is in the first wagon's tail.

"We are three, and ready." His eyes go to the man at the lead mule's head and stay there. "The bar waits on his word."

Pim has stopped by the gate with one hand on the bar's end, his weight already on his back foot. He's watching Bram too.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
Bram grunts at that — the nearest he comes to being caught out.

"Then he's quicker to a yes than he is to a question. Fair enough. Four days to find out which serves him better." He checks the second mule's collar after Pim out of the same habit, finds it tight, and gives the boy a nod that costs nothing and is worth something.

"The post is yours, Master Vosk. You've the paper and the Amnian. I'll stand at the lead team's head and look like a man who's done this before, which is the only thing a corporal wants from a guard. If he asks me anything, it'll be the weather, and I'll tell him it's holding." He glances at the sky to be sure he's not lying. "Dunmore sees the look you've seen off the fence. If the corporal gets curious about the middle wagon, he'll have two men between him and it before he's finished the thought. Not hands on him. Just in the way."

He settles the shield, rests his sword hand on the pommel, and watches the yard door for Pell.

"When he's out, lift the bar. Pim, you did the harness right. Keep doing it that way and someone'll pay you for it one day."

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell nods once and keeps his voice pitched for the yard, not the street beyond. "Off side of the middle wagon, in Bram's sight. Stop when the lead stops. Pass no one." He repeats it the way he'd repeat a contract clause, without impatience, so the factor can hear that it's set.

He glances once down the row to where Bram stands at the lead team's head, then to Pim at the gate. "I saw the upstairs light this morning, but not the woman. If she's not down by now, she's not in." He gives it to Vosk as a simple fact, with no question in it. "It's your run and his line. I walk where I'm put."

Then he steps clear of the first wagon's shadow and makes his way to the middle wagon's far side, the side away from the stable, his feet finding the drier ground by old habit. He chooses a spot a stride back from the rearmost wheel, just ahead of the tailboard and in clear view of the lead team, and lets his cloak settle. One hand rests easy on the strap of his satchel, close to a healing potion if it comes to that; the other hangs loose. His head is up, and his eyes do their slow work: the gate, the tethered mules, the eastern light over the rooftops, the lane beyond the fence.

scenes.narration:
"Then he's quicker to a yes than he is to a question." Bram grunts. "Fair enough. Four days to find out which serves him better."

He goes down to the second lead mule and checks its collar after Pim, out of the same habit as before. The buckle is tight and the strap's tongue is tucked under its keeper. Bram gives the boy a nod. Pim goes red to the ears and looks at the mule instead of at him.

Vosk hears the rest out with the ledger shut under his arm. The post is his, since he has the paper and the Amnian. Bram will stand at the lead team's head looking like a man who has done this before, and if the corporal asks him anything it will be about the weather, which is holding. Vosk follows Bram's glance up at the sky. It is pale and clear over the stable roof, with no cloud anywhere.

"Then we are agreed, Master Halloway. Not hands on him. Only in the way." He says it like a clause he has read back and found sound.

Pell comes down the row and stops by the first wagon. He says the drill back at yard pitch: off side of the middle wagon, in Bram's sight, stop when the lead stops, pass no one. Then he looks at Vosk. "I saw the upstairs light this morning, but not the woman. If she's not down by now, she's not in. It's your run and his line. I walk where I'm put."

"Mistress Marrin is staying in Beregost, Master Dunmore. She told Master Halloway so on the stairs, and she told me last night." Vosk doesn't look at the upper window this time. "So we are three, as I said."

Pell goes round the middle wagon to its far side, away from the stable. He picks his way along the drier ground and stops a stride back from the rear wheel, just ahead of the tailboard, where Bram at the lead can see him down the length of the row. His cloak settles. One hand rests on the strap of the satchel.

*When he's out, lift the bar.* He is out.

"Lift the bar, master. Yes." Pim gets his shoulder under the bar and lays it on the ground without a bang. He drags both leaves of the gate inward, one after the other, and their bottom edges scrape over the packed earth. The Coast Way lies past them, grey-gold in the early light, empty except for a smith's boy with an ash bucket and a dog nosing the gutter. On his way back past the lead team Pim mutters to himself, "Keep doing it that way," and climbs onto the first wagon's bench as if that's where he belongs. He's driving it to the post and walking back. Nobody told him to. Vosk lets it stand.

Vosk climbs onto the middle bench, the one in front of the crate, and gathers the reins. He looks at Bram.

The lead team leans into the collars and the first wagon rolls out under the gate beam onto the road. The middle team goes after it without a toss of the head. A faint hum comes up through the shafts, the same as all night, and the near mule flicks one ear at a fly and nothing more. The third wagon creaks out last. Behind them the yard is empty except for six logs leaning against the fence.

---

They turn north up the Coast Way. Beregost is waking on both sides of the road. Shutters bang open, a forge door rolls back on a bed of coals, and a woman throws a basin of water into the street, then looks hard at the mules as if they'd done it. They pass the cooper's shop with its step empty and go on up the street to the Red Sheaf, which is shuttered tight. Last night's straw has been swept into a heap against its wall and the door is shut. There's nobody on its step and no red cloth anywhere along the street.

The houses thin out past the last smithies. Where the town ends the road narrows between two low stone walls, and across it stands the north post: a lean-to of weathered boards, a pole barrier on a pivot, and a brazier of last night's coals with two men warming their hands over it. They wear the green tabards of the Beregost militia. One is grey and heavy and asleep on his feet. The other is younger, with a corporal's knot on his shoulder and a sergeant's hopes in his face, and he steps out into the road with one hand up before the lead mule's nose has reached the pole.

Vosk climbs down from the middle bench before he's asked. He walks forward with the paper already out, a folded sheet with a stamp in dark wax at its foot, and holds it so the corporal can see the stamp without taking the sheet.

"Gerrit Vosk, cloth factor, out of Nashkel for Baldur's Gate. Three wagons, wool and linen, and two guards. That is my bill for the cargo."

The corporal looks at the stamp for a long moment, the way a man looks at writing he can't read and doesn't want to say so. "Amnian."

"Amnian," Vosk agrees. Three silver pieces have found their way into the hand under the paper. "And this for the road, corporal, with my thanks for the early hour."

The silver goes where silver goes. The corporal walks down the first wagon, as a man does who has been paid and wants it to look like work, and twitches up the canvas at its tail. He finds Orla's oiled bundle, and beside it the spoiled linen bolt, still dark along one edge. He puts two fingers on it.

"Wet."

"Spoiled on the road. It lay against a sweating board," Vosk says, and that's true as far as it goes. "You're welcome to it for a horse-blanket, if you've a use for one."

The corporal snorts and lets the canvas drop. He doesn't go on to the middle wagon. He stops level with the lead team instead and looks Bram up and down: the mended shoulder, the painted-over shield, and the dust of four days ground into his boots that one wash at a trough hasn't touched.

"You came up from Nashkel with this lot?" He jerks his chin south, back down the Way. "Or on your own?"

 *(Out of game, one line each:)*

1) There was no roll, because standing at the lead team's head and watching the yard door couldn't go wrong. Bram stood there until Pell came round the middle wagon, and then the bar came up on his word.

2) There was no roll for this either, since it's just taking up a position. Pell stood a stride back from the middle wagon's rear wheel on the off side, in Bram's sight, and kept that place all the way to the north post.

3) That one wasn't a player's action. Vosk is a person of the world, and he climbed onto the middle bench and took up the reins himself as part of rolling out. Nothing needed a roll.

When you come out of the yard door, the big guard, Bram, is standing at the lead team's head with his shield settled and his sword hand resting on the pommel, watching the door. Vosk stands by with the ledger shut under his arm. Pim waits at the gate.

"Mistress Marrin is staying in Beregost, Master Dunmore. She told Master Halloway so on the stairs, and she told me last night." Vosk doesn't look at the upper window this time. "So we are three, as I said."

You go round the middle wagon to its far side, away from the stable, and stop a stride back from the rear wheel, just ahead of the tailboard, where Bram at the lead can see you down the length of the row.

You are out, and the gate opens.

"Lift the bar, master. Yes." Pim gets his shoulder under the bar and lays it on the ground without a bang. He drags both leaves of the gate inward, one after the other, and their bottom edges scrape over the packed earth. The Coast Way lies past them, grey-gold in the early light, empty except for a smith's boy with an ash bucket and a dog nosing the gutter. On his way back past the lead team Pim mutters something to himself and climbs onto the first wagon's bench as if that's where he belongs. He's driving it to the post and walking back. Nobody told him to. Vosk lets it stand.

Vosk climbs onto the middle bench, the one in front of the crate, and gathers the reins. He looks at Bram.

The lead team leans into the collars and the first wagon rolls out under the gate beam onto the road. The middle team goes after it without a toss of the head. A faint hum comes up through the shafts, the same as all night, and the near mule flicks one ear at a fly and nothing more. The third wagon creaks out last. Behind you the yard is empty except for six logs leaning against the fence.

---

You turn north up the Coast Way. Beregost is waking on both sides of the road. Shutters bang open, a forge door rolls back on a bed of coals, and a woman throws a basin of water into the street, then looks hard at the mules as if they'd done it. You pass the cooper's shop with its step empty and go on up the street to the Red Sheaf, which is shuttered tight. Last night's straw has been swept into a heap against its wall and the door is shut. There's nobody on its step and no red cloth anywhere along the street.

The houses thin out past the last smithies. Where the town ends the road narrows between two low stone walls, and across it stands the north post: a lean-to of weathered boards, a pole barrier on a pivot, and a brazier of last night's coals with two men warming their hands over it. They wear the green tabards of the Beregost militia. One is grey and heavy and asleep on his feet. The other is younger, with a corporal's knot on his shoulder and a sergeant's hopes in his face, and he steps out into the road with one hand up before the lead mule's nose has reached the pole.

Vosk climbs down from the middle bench before he's asked. He walks forward with the paper already out, a folded sheet with a stamp in dark wax at its foot, and holds it so the corporal can see the stamp without taking the sheet.

"Gerrit Vosk, cloth factor, out of Nashkel for Baldur's Gate. Three wagons, wool and linen, and two guards. That is my bill for the cargo."

The corporal looks at the stamp for a long moment, the way a man looks at writing he can't read and doesn't want to say so. "Amnian."

"Amnian," Vosk agrees. Three silver pieces have found their way into the hand under the paper. "And this for the road, corporal, with my thanks for the early hour."

The silver goes where silver goes. The corporal walks down the first wagon, as a man does who has been paid and wants it to look like work, and twitches up the canvas at its tail. He finds Orla's oiled bundle, and beside it the spoiled linen bolt, still dark along one edge. He puts two fingers on it.

"Wet."

"Spoiled on the road. It lay against a sweating board," Vosk says. "You're welcome to it for a horse-blanket, if you've a use for one."

The corporal snorts and lets the canvas drop. He doesn't go on to the middle wagon. He stops level with the lead team instead and looks Bram up and down: the mended shoulder, the painted-over shield, and the dust of four days ground into his boots that one wash at a trough hasn't touched.

"You came up from Nashkel with this lot?" He jerks his chin south, back down the Way. "Or on your own?"

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
I pull the bell-chain once, then step back so I’m plainly visible from the gate, with my hands empty.

If someone answers, I say, “Good morning. Sefa Marrin. I’m seeking Master Thalantyr’s advice about a damaged magical mark I saw on a sealed crate. I haven’t brought the object, only a description. Is he receiving callers, and what would a consultation cost?”

I wait without ringing again or trying the gate.

scenes.input:
(Round 24 — one paragraph per character in this scene. Bram Halloway and Pell Dunmore are elsewhere this round, in a scene of their own that comes to you as its own message: do not narrate them here.)

Sefa Marrin: I pull the bell-chain once, then step back so I’m plainly visible from the gate, with my hands empty.

If someone answers, I say, “Good morning. Sefa Marrin. I’m seeking Master Thalantyr’s advice about a damaged magical mark I saw on a sealed crate. I haven’t brought the object, only a description. Is he receiving callers, and what would a consultation cost?”

I wait without ringing again or trying the gate.
scenes.narration:
Sefa pulls the chain once. The bell is black iron like the gate and has no clapper she can see, but it gives one low, round note that carries over the yew. A moment later the same note comes back from the tower, faint, as if a second bell up there had been struck from the inside. Then both stop. Sefa steps back from the bars with her hands empty and waits.

For a while there's only the smoke going straight up from the chimney and a blackbird working in the frost under the hedge. Then gravel crunches beyond the inner hedge. The steps are slow and even, the steps of a man who doesn't see why he should hurry.

He comes round the corner of the yew: an old man, tall and very thin, in a heavy grey robe with a sheepskin jerkin pulled on over it against the cold. His beard is white and cut short, square across the bottom. He's carrying a clay mug that steams. His left hand has ink on two fingers, old ink worked into the creases, and there's a pair of wire-rimmed lenses pushed up onto his forehead. He stops a pace short of the gate, doesn't open it, and looks at her through the bars the way a man reads the first line of a letter to decide whether to read the rest.

She tells him her name and her business: a damaged mark on a sealed crate, a description and not the object, and she asks whether he's receiving callers and what a consultation costs.

He drinks from the mug before he answers.

"I am receiving you, Mistress Marrin. That's not the same as receiving callers." His voice is dry and exact, with a faint southern edge on some of the vowels, the kind that has worn down over a long time. "You've brought nothing, which is either very sensible or very convenient. I'll find out which."

He lowers the lenses onto his nose and studies her for a moment: the beads at her throat, the pale book at her belt. His eyes stay on the book a breath longer than on anything else, then move back to her face.

"Five gold. For that you get my attention until this mug is cold, and my honest opinion at the end. If I know the mark, you get its name and whatever goes with the name. If I don't, you get my reasons for not knowing. Those are worth less, and you pay the same." He tips the mug a little toward her. "I don't take coin through a gate, and I don't open the gate to someone who hasn't decided. And I'll want to know whose crate, and where it is now. Not to go after it. A mark means one thing on a pedlar's box and another on a Flaming Fist strongbox, and I don't give opinions blind."

He waits, with the steam rising between them and the bar of the gate still in its socket.

"Well? Are you coming in, or did you walk an hour to look at my hedge?"

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
Bram doesn't shift the shield and doesn't look at Vosk. A guard who checks with his factor before answering a corporal is a guard with something to check.

"On my own. Four days up from Nashkel, paid off there, hired on here last night when he was two men short." He says it the way he'd give his name at a tollgate — a fact, not a story. "Road south of here's empty, corporal, if that's worth anything to you. One tinker and one of your patrols the whole way, and the ruts were old. Nobody's running wagons that stretch just now."

He nods at the sky, since he said he would. "Weather's holding. We'd like to make the most of it."

Then he waits, hand resting on the pommel, eyes on the pole barrier and not on the man — the look of someone who's stood at a hundred of these and expects this one to lift like the rest.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell stays where he is on the off side, his eyes drifting past the corporal toward the road ahead and the ditches beyond the post. He doesn't set his hand on his sword; his posture is that of a hired man paid to stand and look about him, and he lets the inspection pass through him like weather. But he's listening, nails in a hinge, and he watches the younger militiaman's knuckles on the pole even while Vosk's silver disappears.

When the corporal stops to study Bram, Pell shifts his weight just enough to bring the length of the middle wagon into his view, and his eyes come back along its near flank. The canvas is tight. The mule hasn't turned its head. Still, he counts the paces from the grey, heavy guardsman to the pole, and the open ground on either side. A man on his side of the road would have to cross the mules. A man behind them, among the last carts and the waking town, would have to go through Pell. He seems in no hurry, and not afraid of boredom.

scenes.narration:
The corporal hears Bram out with his thumbs hooked in his belt. At *the ruts were old* his face changes. He looks less like a man who wants to be sergeant and more like a man adding something up.

"Old ruts." He glances down the road, back the way they came, as if he could see the Nashkel stretch from here. "You're the third this tenday who's told me that. A drover on Fourthday, and a priest on a mule before him." He chews the inside of his cheek. "There's two trains out of Nashkel that should have been through this post by now, and they haven't been. Merchants come up here asking me where their cloth is. Like I'd know." He stops there. It's more than he meant to say to a hired man, and he knows it.

He looks Bram up and down once more: the boots, the mended shoulder, the shield. Then he steps back from the lead mule's nose.

The grey man takes his hands off the coals with a sigh. He leans his weight on the pole's short end, and the long end swings up out of the road on its pivot, creaking.

messages.text:
“I’m coming in. Five gold for an honest opinion is agreed.”

I reach for my purse without approaching the bars.

“The carrier is Gerrit Vosk, a cloth factor. The crate came from Nashkel on commission for a buyer whose name he wouldn’t give me. It was in the Burning Wizard’s yard last night, among three wagons of wool and linen. He intended to leave for Baldur’s Gate at first light. I haven’t witnessed his departure.”

I meet his eyes. “I promised discretion about the seal while he remained in Beregost. The damaged mark is separate from it. I can describe that, the hum, and the unnatural cold without breaking my word. If you need more before you’ll accept the consultation, I’d rather settle that before either of us takes the other’s coin or time.”

scenes.narration:
Sefa's hand finds the purse at her belt and stays there. She doesn't come any closer to the bars.

Thalantyr listens with the mug held under his chin, its steam drifting past the wire lenses. His face doesn't change at *a cloth factor*. At *Nashkel* one white eyebrow lifts a little, and at *I promised discretion about the seal* he lowers the mug.

He drinks before he answers.

"Gerrit Vosk. Cloth, Nashkel to the Gate, and a buyer with no name." He says it back flatly, like a clerk reading a docket. "If he meant first light, he's been an hour on the Coast Way already, so I needn't worry about him knocking on my gate next. That's context enough." He looks at her over the rim. "Keep your word about the seal. It's a sealed box out of Nashkel that a cloth factor won't open and a woman with prayer beads won't talk about. I can guess the colour of the wax without you."

He sets the mug on the flat top of the gatepost. Then he reaches through the bars to the inside bracket, lifts the iron bar out with both hands and leans it against the yew. One leaf of the gate swings inward on hinges that someone keeps oiled.

"In, then. You've decided."

Sefa steps through. The gate closes behind her, and he drops the bar back into its brackets with a short iron knock. Then he holds out his left hand, palm up, with the ink worked into the creases of two fingers.

"Five."

Sefa counts five gold pieces out of her purse into his palm. He goes over them once with his thumb, exactly as he said he would, and they go into the sheepskin jerkin. "Paid." He picks the mug up again. "And the mug's running."

The gravel path runs between two walls of yew clipped as square as the outer hedge, so for a while she walks down a green corridor with frost still white along its shaded side. It turns twice. Then it opens onto a square of garden: herb beds bedded down under straw, a well with a wooden cover, and on the far side the grey tower rising from the earth with its door shut. The sun has cleared the hedge on the eastern side. Along that wall the frost has melted dark on a long stone bench.

Thalantyr sits at one end of it and leaves her the other. As she sits down his eyes go once more to the pale book at her belt, then come away. He says nothing about it.

"It's a cold morning, Mistress Marrin. I'd describe briskly." He wraps both hands round the mug. "The mark first. Where it was on the crate, what made it, and what's left. Tell me only what you saw. If you start telling me what it might have been, I'll stop you."

opening.narration:
Beregost smells of coal smoke and hot iron even in here. Through the shutters comes the steady ring of hammers from the smithies along the Coast Way, and the light is going amber. The Burning Wizard's common room is filling up for the evening: carters, a pair of dusty sellswords, townsfolk with soot still on their forearms. The benches are crowded, and that is how three strangers end up at the same table.

Bram Halloway sits with his back to the wall and his shield propped against the bench, the old company mark painted over. Across from him is Sefa Marrin, a young woman just off the road from Baldur's Gate. Beside her is Pell Dunmore, a lean man from the Lower City with a healer's satchel slung at his hip. He came in by the western road and sat down so quietly that nobody heard him do it.

None of them has said a word to the others yet. Then Orla Tarnwick, the innkeeper, pushes through the crowd with a jug in one hand and three cups hooked on her fingers. She sets them down hard and looks from one face to the next.

"Last free seats in the house, and you three took them together," she says. "So: one tab or three? And what brings each of you into Beregost tonight?"

screens.text:
The session begins.

Beregost smells of coal smoke and hot iron even in here. Through the shutters comes the steady ring of hammers from the smithies along the Coast Way, and the light is going amber. The common room of the Burning Wizard is filling up for the evening: carters, a pair of dusty sellswords, townsfolk with soot still on their forearms. The benches are crowded, and that is how you end up at the same table as two strangers.

You sit with your back to the wall and your shield propped against the bench, the old company mark painted over. Across from you is a young woman who looks freshly in off the road. Beside her is a lean man with a healer's satchel slung at his hip. He sat down so quietly that you never heard him do it.

None of you has said a word to the others yet. Then the innkeeper pushes through the crowd with a jug in one hand and three cups hooked on her fingers. She sets them down hard and looks from one face to the next.

"Last free seats in the house, and you three took them together," she says. "So: one tab or three? And what brings each of you into Beregost tonight?"

Your records:
Bram Halloway — Human, fighter 5 (Champion; Protection fighting style), former caravan guard of the Trade Way, level 5
HP 44/44 · AC 18 · Speed 30 feet
STR 17 · DEX 12 · CON 15 · INT 10 · WIS 13 · CHA 10
Skills: Athletics +6; Perception +4; Survival +4; Intimidation +3; Tools: land vehicles +3
Saves: Strength saving throw +6 (proficient); Constitution saving throw +5 (proficient); Dexterity saving throw +1; Intelligence saving throw +0; Wisdom saving throw +1; Charisma saving throw +0
Attacks: Longsword +6 to hit, 1d8+3 slashing (1d10+3 two-handed); Javelin +6 to hit, 1d6+3 piercing, range 30/120; Extra Attack: two attacks with the Attack action
Abilities: Proficiency bonus +3; Extra Attack: attacks twice when taking the Attack action; Fighting style, Protection: with a shield, a reaction imposes disadvantage on an attack against a creature within 5 feet of him; Second Wind: a bonus action, regains 1d10+5 hit points; once per short rest; Action Surge: one additional action on his turn; once per short rest; Improved Critical (Champion): a weapon attack crits on 19 or 20; Healer's kit: stabilises a dying creature without a check (ten uses)
Limits: No magic at all; Heavy armour: disadvantage on Stealth; Second Wind and Action Surge return only after a short rest
Counters: Hit dice 5/5; Second wind 1/1; Action surge 1/1
Money: 23 gp; 14 sp; 30 cp
Worn: Armor / clothing: Chain Mail; Main hand: Longsword; Off hand: Shield
Pack: Bedroll and Hardtack; Healer's Kit; Hempen Rope (50 feet); Javelin ×4; Tinderbox; Torch ×3

Where you are: shared table, Burning Wizard common room · Time: Day 1 · evening

The woman beside you speaks up. "Three tabs, please. We haven't had time to become bad influences on one another." She eases her pack beneath the bench, clear of everyone's feet. "Sefa Marrin, down from Baldur's Gate. Tonight, supper and a bed are ambition enough. What would those cost?" She turns to include both of you, and her gaze catches for a moment on the quiet man's satchel. "I used to work in a hospice. If either of you has been saving a tale about a blister for someone who can bear to hear it, you've chosen your table well."

The quiet man lets the innkeeper's gaze pass over him a moment before he answers, one hand resting on the table near his cup. "Three," he says easily. "And a cup of whatever's hot." He tips a silver piece onto the table and meets your eyes, then Sefa's. It isn't an unfriendly look, just calm and weighing. "Pell. Passing through." He leaves it there.

The innkeeper doesn't touch the coin until all three of you have spoken. Then she takes your silver, drops four coppers' worth of it into her apron and pushes six coppers back across the wood to you.

"Three tabs. Suits me, less arguing at the end." She points the jug at Sefa. "Supper's mutton stew and black bread, three silver, and it's been on since noon, so it's hot. For a bed it's five silver in the loft, straw and blankets, and you share it with a dozen carters who snore. Eight gets you a room with a door that bolts. Pay in the morning or pay now, just don't pay never."

She looks at Pell's silver, then at him. "Hot means spiced cider, there's a pot by the fire. Five coppers." She takes the coin and counts five coppers back beside his cup without hurrying, like someone who's done it ten thousand times.

Then she turns back to you, and for the first time she looks you over properly: the mended shoulder on your mail, the painted-over shield. "Up from Nashkel, and you've still got your wagon's worth of teeth. That's news here these days. Southbound, nobody's hiring guards, they want twice as many and can't find them." She jerks her chin toward the hearth. A heavy man in a good brown coat sits alone at the end of the long table there, a ledger open beside his bowl. "Northbound, there's Gerrit Vosk. He's a cloth factor, out of Amn by way of Nashkel. He's taking three wagons up to the Gate and he's been short of men since his last pair quit him here two days ago. He didn't tell me why they quit. I didn't ask, and they didn't drink enough to tell me."

Someone across the room shouts for her by name. She sets the jug in the middle of the table.

"Stew, then. Three bowls, unless one of you says otherwise." She's already turning away. "I'll bring the cider."

Your records, changed:
Money: + 26 cp; − 30 cp

Your journal, new:
+ Thread: Guards wanted northbound

Where you are: at a table in the inn's common room · Time: Day 1 · evening

The woman across the table orders stew and the room with a bolt, and counts out eleven silver where the innkeeper can collect it. To your question she says, "A healer, mostly. I can help defend a wagon, though you wouldn't want me holding the shield." She glances toward the cloth factor, then back to you. "I've just come down that road. Not eager to turn straight around, but I'd listen to an offer." She lowers her voice so it stays at your table. "Two guards quitting together might mean trouble on the road, or trouble getting paid. Worth asking which before promising him anything." She leaves Pell's short introduction alone and shifts the jug within everyone's reach. "How was the road up from Nashkel?"

Pell picks up his five coppers and pockets them without looking at them. He leans back a little, not far enough to be careless, and takes in the room over the rim of his cup. "Pell Dunmore," he says to you, as if that's the whole of it. "You like knowing who's on your bench. Now you know as much as I'd tell a friend of an hour." He turns his cup once on the scarred wood and looks at Sefa. "Hospice work, and now the road. That's a long step from clean linen to dust."

Orla comes back through the crowd with a tray on her hip: three bowls of mutton stew with a slab of black bread across each, and a clay mug of cider that steams and smells of clove. She sets the bowls down one at a time and puts the mug in front of Pell.

She sweeps Sefa's eleven silver into her apron and counts it there with her thumb, unhurried. "Stew and the room. Top of the stairs, second door on the left. The bolt's on the inside and it works. That's more than I can say for the one across the hall." She turns to you. "Loft and stew for you makes eight silver. Coin now or on the tab, your choice." To Pell: "Your stew's on yours. Three silver."

Someone at the hearth calls for more bread and she's gone again.

The stew is thick and salty, and the mutton has been cooking long enough to fall apart on the spoon. While you eat, the man at the hearth end of the long table goes on with his business. He spoons stew with his right hand and keeps his left spread flat on the open ledger, as if the room's draught might take the page. You keep watching him without seeming to, and you catch one thing more. The inn's back door opens onto the yard where the wagons stand, and every time it bangs, Gerrit Vosk looks up at it. He doesn't look toward the front door at all. He has done it twice since the bowls came. The second time a stable boy comes in stamping mud off his feet, and Vosk watches him all the way to the kitchen before he goes back to his columns.

Once he glances down the long table to yours, at the shield half under the bench and your mended mail. He holds the look just long enough for it to be a look, then dips his head a fraction, the way a man does across a market when he isn't buying yet. He turns a page.

Sefa's question about the Nashkel road is still waiting for your answer.

Where you are: the inn's common room, at their table · Time: Day 1 · evening

Orla comes past with an empty tray and a full jug. She sweeps your eight silver into her apron without breaking stride. "Loft and stew. Paid." Then she's gone toward the kitchen.

The back door bangs again while you're talking. A carter comes in with a sack of oats on his shoulder, and down at the hearth end the brown coat turns toward the yard once more, and turns back.

Sefa breaks off a piece of bread and answers Pell first. "The linen wasn't always clean. But yes, it's a change." She gives him a small smile. "I wanted to find out what else I could do. So far, mostly walk." She nods to you. "I'll come and hear him out with you after supper. No promise beyond that yet." She takes a few spoonfuls while the stew is hot. Her question comes while you're still rising: "You said you didn't care for how that run ended. Did you find out what you were carrying?" It reaches you as you step clear of the bench, with your shield left behind.

Pell, unhurried, tilts his head at Sefa. "Dust pays better than hospice, if you don't mind the occasional arrow." He turns his spoon in the bowl. "The west road was quiet. A broken cart, a dead snake, nothing worth telling." You're already three steps down the long table when he adds, to Sefa as much as to you: "If you mean to put questions to the factor, I can sit near enough to hear. Not to take work yet, but to know who's hiring, and why."

You stop across the table from Gerrit Vosk. He finishes the spoonful he's on. He closes the ledger over one finger to keep the place, and only then looks up. Close to, he's older than the coat suggests: grey in the beard, a bad night's sleep under each eye, and a ring on his little finger worn down nearly smooth.

He hears you out without interrupting, the first question and then the second. When he answers, he keeps his voice low, under the noise of the room.

"Master Halloway." He says your name carefully, the way a man repeats a figure so he'll remember it. "They wanted more than we had agreed in Nashkel. On this road, this season, every guard south of the Gate thinks he's worth double. I declined, and they declined to go on."

You've heard that answer before, from men who meant it, and this isn't how they say it. It comes out too smooth and too ready, like a line he has gone over on the road. He doesn't look at you while he says it, either. He looks at the finger keeping his place in the ledger.

He seems to know it landed badly. He breathes out through his nose and sets his spoon down in the bowl.

"And the door." His mouth goes tight. "There was also a disagreement about the cargo. One of them took it into his head that what I carry was his business to look at. It is not. A guard's business is the outside of a wagon." He glances at the yard door, and this time he doesn't bother hiding it. "I have three wagons of Amnian wool and linen standing in a yard I don't own, in a town where two men know exactly what's in them and are no longer in my pay. So yes. I watch the door."

He opens the ledger again, flat under his left hand.

"Two gold a day and your food, Master Halloway. Four days to the Gate if the weather holds, and we leave at first light. Half when we start, half at the Basilisk Gate." His eyes go past your shoulder, down the long table to Sefa with her prayer beads and Pell with his satchel. Then they come back. "Those two. Are they with you?"
